The Effect of Urine on Raphanus sativus 
Growth in Lunar Regolith 
Plant the Moon Challenge | Fall 2024 | High School Level 
Bio Cubs | Team #19492 
2024-2025 
 
Tabb High School

INTRODUCTION 
In 2022, NASA scientists managed to effectively grow Arabidopsis Thalian in lunar 
regolith samples —during the Apollo 11, 12, and 17 missions (Keeter 2022). This effectively 
proved that growth in regolith was possible, however, on day six the plants began to show signs 
of struggle and by day 26 the harvested plants were studied, revealing that that plant was in stress 
(Keeter 2022). So why exactly did Arabidopsis Thalian show stress indicating a non-ideal 
environment? Lunar regolith contains many minerals essential for plant growth. However, 
factors such as the lack of nitrogen compounds and the physical composition of the regolith 
makes growing plants difficult. The main minerals needed for plant growth are nitrogen (N), 
phosphorus (P) and potassium(K) while other minor minerals needed include calcium (Ca), 
magnesium (Mg), and sulfur (S). The lack of nitrogen in lunar regolith poses a great issue in 
plant growth in addition to the immense amount of iron content and reactive oxygen species in 
the regolith causing stress to the plant. Furthermore, other factors such as pH, nutrient uptake, 
and moisture values are all outside the ideal range for most crop plants. Studies show that the 
more mature/finer (regolith exposed to harsh cosmic rays and weathering) the regolith, the more 
stress on the plant (Cartier 2022). 
For our experiment we plan to extend NASA’s prior research by targeting all the issues 
uncovered by the plants’ DNA. Specifically, we will be addressing the lack of nitrogen through 
testing the effect of various concentrations of urine:water solutions, a readily accessible 
substance full of nitrogen, on the growth of Raphanus sativus. 
 
Background 
Crimson radish (Raphanus sativus) known for its easy growth, is usually planted in 7.2 to 
29.4 degrees Celsius conditions, requires adequate amounts of water and can flourish in soils that 
are low in nitrogen (Radish: Crimson Crunch). Raphanus sativus needs full sun, takes about 5-7 
days for germination and approximately 28 days for harvest (Renee’s Garden). 
The scarcity of supplies and resources able to be brought into space is extremely difficult. 
So, when considering this, astronauts must use everything to the fullest, this includes their feces 
and urine. Because Earth is running out of phosphorus rock (a major plant nutrient) there comes 
the issue of not how but when we run out of fertilizer for our plants. Urine and feces have been 
used since ancient times as a fertilizer, with urine being pathogen free and known to contain 
more nutrients than human feces. Urine seems to be a valuable resource in solving this issue. 
Urine is rich in nitrogen and phosphorus, both minerals that are lacking in lunar regolith and vital 
for plant growth while also being readily available. 
When our team researched lunar regolith, we found that 98-99% of regolith consist of 
“Oxygen 41-45%, Silicon (Si), Aluminum (Al), Calcium ( Ca), Iron (Fe), Magnesium (Mg),

Titanium (Ti)” while the remaining 1% consist of “ Manganese (Mn), Sodium (Na), Potassium 
(K), Phosphorus (P),” ("The Chemical Composition of Lunar Soil," n.d., para. 2-4). While there 
are “no (=significant amounts of) carbonates, sulfates, or hydrous (water-bearing) minerals on 
the moon,”("The Chemical Composition of Lunar Soil," n.d., para. 7). Furthermore, due to the 
lack of atmospheric oxygen, the common “3+ (ferric) oxidation state” of iron on earth does not 
exist. Most lunar iron closely resembles the iron on the moon, the less common 2+ (ferrous) state 
of iron on Earth and around 10% - is metallic ("The Chemical Composition of Lunar Soil," n.d., 
para. 12). 
As for the pH of the regolith it has an average of 9.6 and a general range of 9-10.5. This 
dramatic increase in alkalinity substantially harms the development of plant organisms, so we 
incorporated Canadian peat moss (pH of 3.0- 4.5) into the growing medium in order to lower the 
pH to the ideal pH of 6 to 7.5. Another thing that stood out during our research is the lack of any 
organic material in regolith and its tendency to compact in the presence of water. By using dried 
chicken manure, peat moss, and coconut coir (little effect on pH) we addressed this problem. 
Plants need carbon, in the form of CO2 to grow. This can be received through human 
breathing however, considering efficiency it would be best to use a CaCO 3

Question 
What concentration of urine will provide the best nutrients and acidity to stabilize the 
regolith and allow the radish grow to its full potential? 
 
Hypothesis 
If the urine combined with amendments to the regolith, results in a high pH , then it will 
neutralize the regolith and allow the plant to grow to its greatest capacity. 
 
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN 
Experimental Abstract 
The inhospitable conditions of lunar regolith, including its elevated alkalinity and 
absence of essential nutrients, presents a substantial challenge for sustainable plant growth to 
nourish space exploration. This experiment investigates the potential benefits of human urine as

a natural, available solution for improving the livability and fertility of lunar regolith. Containing 
vital nutrients including nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, as well as an acidic pH, urine 
substantiates the pursuit of neutralizing the alkalinity of lunar regolith and rejuvenating the 
plants’ wellbeing. In this study, simulated lunar regolith was treated with various concentrations 
of human urine, and Raphanus Sativus plants were cultivated under surveillance and controlled 
conditions. 
Ultimately, the data from this experiment suggests that urine could play a critical role in 
elevating plant agriculture on the Moon, eventually contributing to long-lasting life support 
systems for long-term space exploration missions. Further analysis is needed to advance 
understanding of the effect of urine treatments on the long-term effects on plant health. 
 
Experimental Parameters 
In this experiment assessing the potential of utilizing urine to neutralize alkalinity and 
enhance nutrient deficiencies in lunar regolith for plant growth, there are several experimental 
parameters crucial to its development. The concentration of urine applied to the regolith 
simulant, expressed as urine:water ratios ranging from 0.081 to .127, is the independent variable 
being tested on Raphanus Sativus. Additionally, the age of the person sourcing the urine is an 
independent variable. The dependent variables include the height, stem width, number of leaves, 
and leaf coloration. The controlled variables accentuate the effects of urine and included 
fertilizer type, growing container, light exposure, watering frequency, measuring frequency, seed 
source, plant species, and temperature. Finally, the incisive and compact ranges of urine 
concentrations allow for thorough investigation of urine’s effectiveness on plant growth, 
necessitating extensive efforts to minimize uncontrolled variables such as bacterial 
contamination that potentially alter experimental results.

Control 
Our 3-control pots will be using miracle grow potting mix to showcase the growth of 
Raphanus sativus in normal earth conditions with no soil additives and only be watered with 
plain water (40ml). Frequence of watering will be every other day like the test plants. 
 
PROCEDURES

Planting Procedures 
Begin by preparing the simulated lunar regolith (lunar soil), making sure that each 
container receives a consistent amount of regolith, along with measured amounts of soil additives 
such as dried chicken manure, peat moss, gypsum, and coconut coir. Make sure each Raphanus 
sativus seed will be planted at a depth of 6-8 mm ensuring that each container receives a 
consistent amount of regolith. For consistency, one seed will be planted per pot. Each pot will be 
labeled according to its specific group (ex: urine concentration or control). Once labeled, the pots 
will be watered with 40 mL of the corresponding water-to-urine mixture . The pots will then be 
placed in a growth chamber, where they will receive equal exposure to controlled light and 
temperature conditions throughout the experiment. 
 
Watering Procedures 
Water is vital for all plants to grow and survive. Water comprises up to 9.5% of a plant’s 
tissue. It is needed for a seed to sprout and is responsible for carrying nutrients throughout the 
plant as the plant grows. It is also necessary for other important processes in plants such as 
photosynthesis, cell structural support, and transpiration (Richmond). In this experiment, 
however, pure water will not be used to hydrate the plants but rather solutions of varying 
concentrations of water and urine. The procedure for watering the experimental plants is, (or 
will be) as follows. Team members will add 40 ml of urine concentration to the plants. The urine 
will then be diluted with the water at a ratio ranging from 0.081 to .127. The urine should not be 
applied on leaves or other parts of the plants because it could cause foliar burning and create 
consumption issues. The urine concentration will be added to the plants every other day at 10:15 
am. 
 
Light Procedures 
The Moon has a day-to-night cycle of about 29.5 earth days (On every orbit- moon gets 
about 2 weeks’ worth of daylight/nighttime (each 14.75 days)). A plant’s exposure to sunlight 
intensity and time will differ from the Earth. The use of LED lighting ensures that it provides an 
efficient amount and exposure to different wavelengths of light. Blue, as well as red, to aid plants 
in photosynthesis. The following steps could be a part of the experiment’s procedure. First, 
position the light above each pot containing Raphanus sativus (The growth chamber in the 
science hallway of Tabb High School will be used to control the time and temperature to ensure 
correct lunar atmosphere simulation). Instead of imitating the lunar day-to-night cycle, exposing 
Raphanus sativus to light for 12 continuous hours in a 24-hour period will be conducted 
(Simulating the 12-hour days and 12-hour nights in 29.5 earth days to lunar cycle). The growth 
chambers will be controlled to set the timer to expose each pot to 12 hours of LED light. After 
the 12-hour cycle for the lunar day ends, the growth chambers will be set to turn off the LED

lights for 12 hours in order to replicate the lunar night (8:00 AM start, lights turn on / 8:00PM 
stop, lights turn off). LED lights will need to be at full intensity in order to mimic the sunlight on 
the surface of the moon, which can be done through the use of Full-spectrum LED bulbs and 
LED lights with a high CRI of 90+. The atmosphere will maintain the temperature within a range 
of 20-25C (68-77F) for the Lunar Daytime temperatures. An approximate range of 15-20C (59-
68F) during simulated lunar nighttime temperatures will ensure the plant’s growth. The 
experiment will be conducted with the management of 12-hour lunar cycles for 33~35 days in 
accordance with the experiment duration: 
- 
Minimum duration: 5 days germination period+28 days= 33 days 
- 
Maximum duration: 7 days germination period+28 days=33 days 
 
 
 
Measurement Procedures 
Various methods will be used to measure several factors and dependent variables within 
the experiment. Measurements of the plant, soil chemistry(pH), atmosphere, etc. will be taken 
every day at 10:15am. Plant measurements will include the height of the plant, the diameter of 
the stem, and the leaf lengths, measured with a centimeter ruler. The number of leaves will be 
observed. The soil and atmospheric data will be measured using pH monitors/pH strips and a 
humidity monitor respectively. 
 
Possible Confounding Variables 
 
Gender differences in the experiment can be considered one of the confounding variables 
as women’s urine contains progesterone and estrogen metabolites, while male urine has 
testosterone. Since females have shorter urethra, they have a higher percentage of urinary tract 
infections. Furthermore, in male urine, there is a high percentage of creatinine since they have 
high muscle mass. With different factors, these hormonal differences could influence the lunar 
soil’s reaction and radish absorption. 
 
When a person gets older, there are changes in the urinary system. Thus, urine 
concentration could be a factor because of water intake, and creatinine levels. As people age 
metabolism tends to slow down and urea becomes an important contributor to concentrated 
urine. In the elderly, there are potential issues with protein malnutrition as “during the past 
decade, the genes that encode two urea transporters (UT-A and UT-B) were cloned” (Sands 11). 
UT-A is located on chromosome 18 and “... is expressed in the apical membrane of the inner 
medullary collecting duct, and vasopressin rapidly increases both UT-A1 phosphorylation and 
urea transport” (Sands 11). According to Sands, research on aged rats indicated “a reduction in

UT-A1 abundance could decrease urea reabsorption across the inner medullary collecting duct, 
thereby reducing inner medullary interstitial urea accumulation, which would in turn reduce 
urine-concentrating ability. In UT-A1 abundance, it could lead to a reduced inner medullary 
interstitial urea accumulation, which decreases the urine-concentrating ability” (Sands 11). 
 
Health conditions such as infections, genetic diseases, diabetes, urinary tract infection 
(UTI), and other factors could lead to decreasing soil balance and results could differ. Infections 
such as “bladder infections such as cystitis, seen almost exclusively in young women” (Dirks J, 
Remuzzi G, Horton S, et al. 13). Males “are less susceptible to acute, uncomplicated infections 
of the bladder or the kidney, with an incidence of five to eight episodes per 10,000 men 
annually” (Dirks J, Remuzzi G, Horton S, et al. 13). For diabetics, one of “the earliest sign of 
diabetic nephropathy is the appearance of small amounts of protein in the urine (proteinuria). As 
proteinuria increases and blood pressure rises, kidney function declines” (Dirks J, Remuzzi G, 
Horton S, et al. 25). As a result, there could be the presence of bacteria in the urine sample, 
an increase of white blood cells, high acidity from diabetes, and dehydration, leading to urine 
being more concentrated. 
 
The pH of urine could depend on the individual’s diet and medications as it is between 
acidic and alkaline. A diet with more consumption of “high fruit and vegetable intake and lower 
consumption of meat was significantly associated with a more alkaline urine pH before and after 
adjustment for age” (Welch, Alisa A. et al. 1). Diet becomes an important contributor as there are 
“alkaline salts in fruit and vegetables, that also supply large amounts of Mg and K in the diet” 
(Welch, Alisa A. et al. 3). As a result, it reflects the urine pH and the kidney function. This 
additionally ties back to underlying health conditions such as UTI, and medications and 
supplements such as calcium, diuretics for high blood pressure, vitamin D to absorb calcium, 
which increases the calcium level in the urine, iron supplements, as too much can be toxic and 
cause radishes to overconsume iron. 
 
EXECUTION AND PROJECT NOTES 
We began by measuring precise amounts of lunar regolith and chicken manure using a 
digital scale. These components were combined to replicate lunar agriculture conditions. Then, 
urine solutions with concentrations ranging from 3.0 to 4.5 were prepared using a micropipette. 
Each solution was stored in labeled beakers, which were tightly sealed with plastic wrap to 
minimize contamination and prevent evaporation. These beakers were kept in a refrigerator to 
maintain a consistent pH level throughout the experiment. 
For plant growth, 2 oz small plastic containers served as the planting pots. Each container 
was cut with three 1-inch slits on the bottom to allow proper drainage. This ensured optimal 
conditions for plant root development. To water,2 we used a pipette to pour exact amounts of 
water or urine concentrations directly to the growing medium. This approach minimized waste 
and ensured uniformity across all samples.

Planting Method 
The planting methods employed in our first experiment consisted of multiple steps that 
were performed with precision and care. The first step taken was using a scale to measure 45 
grams of the regolith mixture into cups with three slits. These slits were 2.5 cm in length on the 
bottom side of the cup, and we used a box cutter to slice them. We then used an iron nail to 
create multiple punctures at the bottom of the cup for further drainage. Next, we patted down the 
soil in the cup gently with the pad of our thumbs, and we used a #2 pencil to lightly create 3 
indentations that measured to be the depth of the eraser end. We then inserted one seed into the 
cup per indentation and using the end of the pencil, we gently pushed the surrounding soil 
towards the indentation to cover it. After this process, we lightly patted on the soil like before to 
cover and smooth everything up. We then proceeded onto the watering and watered each plant 
with 6 mL of water for moisture. We placed a humidity dome, which was a plastic container with 
a lid and a small opening located in the center of the container, over the tray of pots in order to 
reduce evaporation and promote germination. The plants were consistently watered with distilled 
water until sprouts appeared, allowing us to begin manipulating our IV. 
 
Beginning of Experiment 
The plants were left in a growth chamber at 80 degrees Fahrenheit, although this raised 
issues with overheating and combined with oversaturation of the plants during the first planting, 
making the seeds unable to germinate. Errors in the original planting such as plants being too 
hastily sowed and the soil being too compact are also believed to be factors in the seeds' inability 
to germinate. After a week in which zero seeds successfully germinated, the decision was made 
to replant the seeds and restart the experiment on Friday. The same methods were used; however, 
it was approached more carefully to ensure no mistakes were made and the seeds had the chance 
to germinate. The pH was consistent at 8, which was too high for optimal growth. The sprouted 
seeds were moved to a new growth area, in which it was set on a wooden platform raised about 1 
meter above the ground using a stand, which had a LED light above the plants—about 0.20 
meters above the metal tray that held the plants. The LED was set on a timer that was turned on 
from 8am to 8pm every day. The temperature and humidity would have been approximately the 
same as the room they were held in, with respective data on the excel sheet. 
 
Replanting – Modifications 
To ensure the germination of the replant, the team considered the only data collected 
during the week of lack of growth: pH, which had been constantly in the range of 8-9. To solve 
this issue, Candian peat moss was added to the regolith until the pH measured the ideal 6. 
Furthermore, observations were made regarding the excessive compactness, which likely caused

difficulty in seed germination and growth of the root system. This led to concluding the need to 
add more coconut coir to the mixture to increase aeration. After adjustments were made to the 
soil, each cup was precisely filled with 45 grams of soil, seeded, and planted by one member to 
ensure consistency.

Experiment Progression 
During the experimental process, all the plants sprouted on the third day, confirming 
successful seed germination. The plants were initially watered with 6ml of urine concentration 
every two days until germination was achieved. The initial watering amount was increased to 10 
ml every other day, then to 20ml every other day, and finally, the watering process was adjusted 
to follow a standard of 15ml every other day, based on the observed plants’ needs. 
Unfortunately, one missed watering session led to the death of several plants in the experiment, 
specifically plants that were given a higher concentration of urine- (3.8, 4.1, 4.2, and 4.5). This 
revealed which specific plant concentrations were susceptible to drought . Remarkably, multiple 
seeds from one concentration type endured, which indicated a stronger resistance to adverse 
conditions. Some plants had all three sprouts from each trial survive while others had fewer, 
demonstrating varying degrees of germination among the different urine concentrations. 
Following the death of certain plants, there was a growing proliferation of algae within the 
plastic cups, suggesting that the regolith mixture simulating the moon’s environment retained the 
nutritional capacity to sustain life. An appropriate watering schedule was adapted again based on 
the plants’ requirements, beginning with 10ml after 4 weeks, increasing to 20ml two weeks later,

and then decreasing to 15ml after an observation that 20ml was excessive for the plants. The 
plants looked severely overwatered and were drooping, likely due to inadequate drainage despite 
multiple punctures made into the container. The observations collected throughout the 
experiment align with NASA’s research, which also documented a growth in similar small 
containers by day 6. However, plants in our experiment showed a more positive effect on 
growth, enduring significantly longer despite growing in similar small containers. This indicates 
the potential improvements in growth conditions conducted in our experiment which influenced 
plant resilience. In conclusion, this experiment emphasized the critical importance of precise 
waterins schedules and concentrations in sustaining plant growth. 
 
Errors – Confounding Variables 
Confounding variables encountered during this experiment included: a day of watering 
was forgotten, a day that plants were watered with 20 mL instead of 6 mL, another day where 
plants were scheduled to be watered 6 mL but were watered 10 mL. Moreover, another 
confounding variable is that it was growing in a room where the lights were occasionally turned 
off, and students in the classes could mess with it. While watering, some members would be 
holding the containers possessing the plants. Thus, the pressure of holding it might have led to 
cracks in the soil mass and the formation of paths where water would go, leaving some parts dry 
and more saturated. Due to missing one watering day, some plants were too dry, and some were 
not draining immediately. Though the research had many confounding variables, it did not 
detract from certain plants flourishing for specific concentrations.

Qualitative Observations 
During our experiment, the team made a plethora of observations to make minor 
adjustments to enhance plant growth. To base, for modifications in the experiment regarding 
watering and minor details and lighting distance to ensure the plant’s most optimal growth. Some 
observations include stark contrasts between the experimental group (watered with urine: water 
concentration on regolith mixture) and the control (watered with distilled water on Miracle-Gro- 
Potting Mix). 
 
▪ Despite excessive watering during the first week of growth that led to replanting, there 
seemed to be no growth of mold, while the smell of the process of anaerobic bacterium 
(lack of air and excess moisture leads to an anaerobic bacterium which results in toxins 
being released into the soil to prevent plant growth) was present instead.

▪ Excessive moisture leads to the growth of algae in areas such as the top of the regolith 
and areas of drainage. 
▪ All plant containers had the same number of slits and punctures for drainage; however, 
some containers drained immediately while others did so relatively slowly. 
▪ From the start of growth, the experimental group (EG) had been a shade darker than that 
of the control group (CG) 
▪ The development of seed leaves (leaves that help support the leaf in gaining nutrients to 
form permanent leaves) of the EG had been significantly prolonged compared to the CG, 
whose seed leaves died a few days in. After observing for a multitude of days, the seed 
leaves of EG died when the radish was visibly forming. 
▪ EG had grown significantly more leaves than the CG. 
▪ The plants thrived under the moisture cap. 
▪ When the plants displayed signs of overwatering, the stem would darken and wilt overall. 
▪ All surviving plants, aside from concentration 4.4, had a slight purple tip, indicating 
phosphate deficiency. 
▪ Visible buildup of possible salts from urine in the slits for drainage resulting from over 
saturation of some plants. 
 
Data Analysis 
 
▪ One missing watering day on 10/25 lead to the death of concentration: 3.4:36.6, 3.8:36.1, 
4.1: 35.9, 4.2:36.8 
▪ Plants of concentration: 3.1:36.9, 3.6: 36.4, 4:36 height on data indicate significant 
decline in height however, this is due to the plants needing more water so height indicates 
drooping but not death 
▪ Week 4 : increase in growth due to increase of watering amount 
▪ Week 4: EG plants are no longer growing taller while its leaves are growing bigger and 
stems significantly thicker stems than CG 
▪ Week 6: 12/6/24 snipping of inferior plants of the three per cup led to those with thinner 
stem IV groups to develop thicker stems 
▪ Remaining surviving EG plants have all produces a small radish approximately 25 mm 
long and 6.35 thick in diameter 
▪ No growth of radishes in CG aside from extensive root system 
▪ Some of CG leaves had red tips indicating lack of phosphate 
 
Discussion 
This research aims to determine if the usage of urine concentration would benefit crimson 
crunch radish (Raphanus sativus) growth in lunar regolith, specially when the regolith is 
modified to conditions for ideal plant growth, resembling earth’s soil. An additional aim is to 
determine what concentration of urine would ould result in the best radish plant. From the data,

there shows to be immediate rapid growth of the EG when compared with the CG (watered and 
grown in soil of regular conditions). Furthermore, considering qualitative observations the EG 
had significantly thicker stems compared to the CG throughout the experiment indicating a 
strong foundation for radish development. While the significant number of leaves produced by 
the EG suggests that the urine concentrations had modified the growth of the plant increasing its 
ability to intake sunlight and create nutrients. This likely in conjunction with the phosphates and 
nitrogen in the urine led to speeding up the growth of Raphanus sativus. This is further proven 
by the growth of the radish plant in the EG and no apparent radish in the CG. The extensive 
growth of the radish plant was also abnormal when compared to the past planting in such 
methods as stated by our mentor. In past cases of planting of seeds in small containers and of 
such environment has only resulted in about 50-80% sprouting whereas in this research the 
percentage of seed germination far surpassed this average. Moreover, in past plantings crops 
were only set to grow for a set 2-3 days and later replanted into the garden otherwise there was a 
high likelihood of no complete development in such small containers. From the results of the 
data from this research, it is likely concludable to assume that the minerals of the lunar regolith 
and from the urine could have helped increase the livelihood of the plants and encourage early 
root development. This can be helpful in advancing not just space agriculture but also here on 
earth since the root development of the radish in the EG suggests a possible significance in 
mineral beneficiation in plant growth. 
In the line graph of the overall growth of the radish plant, when considering the sudden 
deaths of plants due to improper watering by human error and looking towards those that 
survived, it is inferable that in the situation and condition of optimal watering quantities and 
frequency there is a high likelihood the EG would flourish even more over the CG and provide 
this research an alternate end data. Whereas limitations of the experiment include the size of the 
cup which limited the growth of the radish as in the end each plant had grown an extensive root 
system. 
The result of what distinct concentration is most optimal for plant growth on lunar 
regolith when considering qualitative observations (leaf quality, leaf coloration, stem width and 
radish size) deems concentration 3.1:36.9 the most favorable for plant development. However, 
due to the range of outlying variables this research would require further testing to confirm this 
statement. 
Conclusion 
This study investigates the effectiveness of urine on the growth of Raphanus sativus on 
lunar regolith. The team's findings prove that urine concentrations enhance and encourage life 
growth on lunar regolith. Suggesting the importance of nutrients through a variety of sources 
vital in aiding the development of a plant in the harsh conditions of the Moon. Furthermore, it 
addresses the scarcity issue of space travel and energy consumption through testing the most 
accessible resource available: urine. At the same time, it highlights the importance of the aeration 
of the regolith, its water retention, pH, and nutrient distribution. The challenges of watering

faced by the team and its effects on the plant's growth emphasize the necessity of precise 
watering. 
Overall, our study and research recommend further investigation: into the implications of 
an individual's health effect on urine samples for watering, methods of accurately determining 
needs for watering, the period length of growing a full radish in such conditions compared to 
ones on earth, taste of radish, nutrient of crimson radishes grown on lunar regolith, and the 
effects of differing growth habits of Raphanus Sativus such as its seed leaves. 
By thinking outside the box, our study highlights a unique approach toward space 
agriculture in hopes of opening a new path toward enhancing the knowledge and ability of 
agriculture on the Moon.

FURTHER INVESTIGATION 
 
Result of Concentration of Urine on the Growth of Radish 
In our first experiment, we found that the 3.1:36.9 urine concentration produced the best results. 
Plants in this group reached an average height of 54 mm and had more true leaves compared to 
other concentrations. Based on these findings, we used the 3.1 concentration for all plants in our 
second experiment to test its effectiveness across different ages. 
 
Background 
The primary goal of this experiment was to take the experiment further by observing the 
potential impact of urine concentrations from varying age groups on plant growth in a lunar 
environment. We hypothesized that an individual’s age might play a specific role in aiding plant 
growth. We recognized that various factors such as the human volunteers’ hormonal levels and 
overall nutritional intake could potentially affect the compositional makeup of urine- resulting in 
potential differences in overall plant growth. Considering that the majority of the astronauts in 
space missions have historically been male, the experiment aimed to gain male human 
volunteers. This decision allowed our group to align our research with possible profiles of 
astronauts likely to be encountered by future lunar mission crews on the moon. 
 
Question: 
Does the age of the donor affect the growth of Raphanus Sativus? 
 
Hypothesis: 
If the ages between 18-30 are fully developed and at their peak age for health, then their plants 
will flourish and be the healthiest compared to the other age groups. 
 
Experiment Setup

In this experiment, we followed the same procedure as before. The cups had three slits 
and drainage holes. Each water-to-urine concentration was made from specimen urine cups with 
different ages, using concentration 3.1, 36.9. After adding the mixtures to individual beakers and 
covering them with saran wrap, each cup was filled with lunar regolith and 3 Raphanus sativus 
seeds. Lastly, each cup was watered with 6 mL of distilled water. 
 
Experimental Design 
Soil additives and different volumes of water were used to water the plants every other 
day. Lighting source and the seed species used were the same—this experiment took place on 
the same stand as the first one, having overlapped experimental windows. The 2nd experiment 
was shorter than the first, however, and the controls were planted in the same regolith mixture 
but watered with water. During the 4 weeks, the amount of water used changed from 10mL every 
other day to 20mL every other day and then modified to 15ml based on need. At approximately 
10am every day, team members were to water the plants with the decided quantity of water. 
 
Independent Variable 
Ages: 16, 18, 21, 22, 35, 41, 44, 55, 54, 65 
 
Confounding Variables 
For this experiment, we started the control group later, which affects the baseline for 
comparing them while not being in the same timeframe. The timing introduces a difference in 
growth, light, and temperature conditions that influence the plant to develop independently 
during the experiment. From this, the delay creates a late start on the developmental stage during 
observation and data that could lead to misleading conclusions. Furthermore, the controls we had 
cannot provide an accurate point of our comparison as the experimental group was experiencing 
the sprouting stage, while the control group could still be germinating. Other factors such as the 
soil moisture from week to week and humidity can affect the data, making changes in growth 
conditions. Overall, this observation may cause some issues in finding patterns or factors that are 
causing both the experimental and control groups. 
In the experiment, the age of the men and their urine could have affected the growth 
outcomes of the seeds. As urine can vary with age, with younger men have higher concentrations 
of hormones like testosterone, which could provide more nutrients to stimulate plant growth. 
However, older men could produce urine with different chemical compositions, which could 
potentially decrease the sprouting of the plants. As urea provides nitrogen, high concentrations 
(dehydration) of urine can cause nitrogen overload (nutrient burn) and higher levels of salt, 
which results in stressing the plants. This also creates an effect on soil acidity and less

availability of nutrients. In contrast, a low concentration (hydrated) urine faces better nutrient 
uptake and is less likely to harm the plants, with beneficial nutrient absorption. As a result, plants 
that received urine from younger men tended to be more successful and had a higher germination 
rate. While the others died from excess nitrogen, which kills the plants, and due to the lower 
levels of testosterone found in older men, this can influence their urine composition of nitrogen.

Qualitative Observation 
Throughout watering days, members note various observations from coloration, leaf size, stem 
diameter, and damage to draw conclusions and modify the treatment of the plants as needed. 
Main observations include: 
▪ Plant growth is exponentially faster than in the prior experiment. 
▪ When sprouting plant roots were visible such uprooting is likely due to erosion from 
improper watering of the first 6ml which likely was directed of the seeds rather than 
around the perimeter. 
▪ Plants show similar growth patterns as prior experiment with stable growth in terms of 
height which periodically becomes stagnant as it uses its nutrients to grow foliage. 
▪ Plants experienced a direct decline in development when watering went from 10ml to 
20ml despite dry soil towards the end of the 10ml watering period. 
▪ Despite precise measurements, CG soil is lower in height to the EG, this difference in soil 
height could result in CG plants growing taller due to need rather than as development 
which can skew interpretations of data 
Data Analysis 
▪ The EG collectively has a steady exponential growth for the week 1, while average of EG 
on data performs better in growth (This can be inaccurate due to the delay in planting of 
CG) 
▪ Overall decline on 11/23/24 for unknown reasons likely related to watering and moisture 
levels. 
▪ Transition to 20ml during end of week 3 and week 4 results in the deaths of multiple 
plants while some were able to survive despite excess moisture and were able to revive 
after modifications of watering to 15ml. 
▪ Data by end of week 4 concludes that age 16 led to the most optimal plant growth 
 
Discussion

The study aims to explore the effects of an individual’s age for urine concentrations on the 
growth of Raphanus sativus. From the data, the usage of 3.1 concentration is shown to 
effectively grow Raphanus sativus which supports the prior experiment about the effectiveness 
of urine concentration on plant growth. However, due to the short growth period for this 
experiment, there was not adequate time for a radish to develop, so interpretation will solely be 
based on the visible plant. Ultimately, the average growth of the EG had been greater than the 
CG. By the end of the four weeks the surviving plants included: control 1, 2, 3, plant age: 16, 28, 
and 41 with dry soil. At the meantime, the remaining had died due to over saturation with them 
showing symptoms of wilting, darkening and purple stems while the soil remained moist in the 
days leading up to their deaths. 
Our quantitative data shows that age16 had the most significant growth overall, with 
57mm in height by the end of the 4 weeks and 13 leaves. Followed by the age 28, with a 51 mm 
height and 5 leaves. With the average of 48 mm of height by the end of the experiment when not 
including dead plants. 
In terms of foliage, by the end of the study age 16 had the most leaves of a total of 13, 
further supporting the result of age 16 as the most optimal for Raphanus sativus growth. While 
the overall average number of leaves grown EG vs. CG, results in the CG have more leaves of an 
average of 10.33 and an average of 8.66 for EG when not considering the dead plants. Although, 
when considering the foliage when the plants were still alive it shows that the EG had a 
converging point where they began to have similar number of leaves and rate of growth. These 
results conclude that age 16 has the greatest growth. However, due to challenges in water it is 
difficult to confidently state age 16 as the most optimal for Raphanus sativus growth. 
 
 
Conclusion 
Our hypothesis was not supported by the results of the experiment. As ages 18-30 for the 
majority had died aside from age 28. However, when considering the height before its death they 
remain only half of the height of age 16. For example, week 4, the first measurements of the 
week for age 16 is 44 while age 18 was 0, and age 21 was 23. 
The result of the study further proves the effectiveness of concentration 3.1:36.9 in the 
growth of Raphanus sativus as the average growth of plant when not considering those that died 
in the process were taller by about 3mm. Due to the errors in watering it, and basing 
interpretations on the ones that survived, the data shows inconsistency in survival because of the 
wide range in ages of surviving plants in the end. 
From our studies and research further investigation is recommended in the fields of 
testing of whether gender could play a factor, if hormones might actively affect the growth of 
Raphanus sativus, and what would be an effective watering plan.
